title: HarnessLLM: Rust Verification Harness Generation with Large Language Models
abstract: Rust’s ownership and type system offer strong memory safety guarantees, but unsafe code and runtime panics still present significant risks. Formal verification is essential to ensure memory safety, but developing verification harnesses remains a challenging and manual task. Although large language models (LLMs) have shown strong performance in various code analysis tasks, directly applying them to harness generation often results in inaccurate API invocations, inefficient nondeterministic data generation, and fabricated fixes.

title: Designing Systems with Digital Twins and AI Agents
abstract: The integration of Digital Twins and AI Agents is reshaping how smart systems are designed and operated across domains such as manufacturing, healthcare, and smart infrastructures. Digital Twins provide real-time virtual representations of physical systems, while AI Agents enable autonomy and adaptive decision-making. Together, they enhance monitoring, prediction, and optimization capabilities. This technical brief introduces a systematic, domain-driven approach for architecting systems that combine Digital Twins with AI Agents. It outlines how to model and synchronize relationships between physical and virtual entities and presents novel design patterns addressing key challenges, including real-time synchronization, scalability, interoperability, and AI-driven automation. Through illustrative case studies, the session demonstrates how these principles can be applied across industries to build resilient, adaptive, and intelligent systems. Attendees will gain practical insights into designing Digital Twin architectures that effectively integrate IoT, AI, and data analytics to meet the demands of modern digital transformation.

title: NotDec: WebAssembly Decompilation With Inter-Procedural Type Recovery
abstract: With WebAssembly widely supported in browsers, containers, IoT devices, and serverless platforms and increasingly adopted as a universal low-level bytecode standard, auditing its hidden vulnerabilities and malicious intentions has become critical. Decompiling existing WebAssembly modules can help security researchers and end users understand binary behavior, but current tools suffer from verbose result, poor readability, and limited type recovery. We present NotDec, an advanced WebAssembly decompilation framework. NotDec extends the WebAssembly type checking algorithm to lift bytecode into an SSA-based IR, applies the inter-procedural type recovery algorithm Retypd with pointer and numeric value differentiation methods to recover complex data structures, and leverages Memory SSA alongside semantics-preserving structured control-flow analysis to emit readable, semantically consistent C code. NotDec achieves 100% recompilation success rate on all 5,241 Juliet samples and all Howard dataset programs, significantly outperforming baselines including Ghidra (45.95% success rate). On type recovery accuracy, NotDec recovers 85.33% of struct member accesses in real-world programs, vastly exceeding Ghidra's 9.24%. While the full inter-procedural version faces scalability challenges on large binaries, the intra-procedural variant NotDec_F demonstrates superior efficiency, consuming less than half of Ghidra's memory and up to 97% less execution time on unoptimized binaries.

title: XRFix: Exploring Performance Bug Repair of Extended Reality Applications with Large Language Models
abstract: As an emerging technology, Extended Reality provides end-users with an immersive experience of interacting with virtual and physical environments. Unlike traditional software, the execution of XR applications involves more computationally complex operations, such as 3D scene rendering, real-time animation, and process simulations. Inefficient coding practices during the software development of XR applications may cause various performance bugs, degrading user experience and even causing motion sickness. Thus, it is an urgent need to develop an automated program repair framework for fixing performance bugs in complex XR programs. However, it is non-trivial to achieve this goal due to several technical challenges: (1) a lack of a real-world XR codebase and bug dataset, (2) no accurate bug detection tool, and (3) no effective bug-fixing tool designed for XR performance bugs. To tackle these challenges, we present a novel large language model-based framework, namely XRFix, to repair performance bugs for open-source XR programs. We first construct a corpus of domain-specific performance bugs built with a codebase from 23 open-source XR projects and a dataset of XR-related bugs containing 104 real-world bugs. Then, we tailor two static analysis tools for accurately detecting bugs in both C# scripts and asset files. Last, we design different prompts to instruct LLMs to fix XR bugs in three types of bug scenarios with different complexities, i.e., single-line level, function level, and class level. We conduct extensive experiments on five off-the-shelf LLMs to evaluate the bug-fixing performance of XRFix. We also compare our XRFix with three SOTA APR approaches. Through static analysis, reference answer comparison, and manual inspection, we demonstrate that our XRFix can effectively fix XR bugs, outperforming SOTA APR methods.

title: DBcover: A White-box SQL Test Generation Framework for Coverage Improvement
abstract: Relational Database Management Systems (RDBMSs) are the backbone of modern data-intensive applications, making reliability and robustness critical. However, achieving high coverage in RDBMS testing remains challenging because of large codebases and complex execution logic. Traditional fuzzing relies on random SQL generation and cannot capture the correspondence between SQL inputs and internal execution paths, while symbolic execution suffers from prohibitive cost and scalability limitations. We propose DBcover, an LLM-driven white-box SQL test generation framework based on contextual reasoning. DBcover uses lightweight dynamic analysis to extract SQL-to-path correspondence and call graphs as global context, and collects source-level information around target functions as local context. These contexts are organized in a unified knowledge graph for efficient retrieval and reuse. DBcover then performs two-phase test generation: it first selects a semantically relevant seed whose execution path is close to the uncovered target, and then guides the LLM with global and local context to generate SQL test cases that trigger previously uncovered code regions. Experiments show that DBcover achieves 80.1% and 82.3% coverage on PostgreSQL and MySQL, and is also effective on the enterprise RDBMS KingbaseES, demonstrating its practical applicability to closed-source systems.

title: Breaking the Alphabet: Rethinking File Ordering in Code Review
abstract: Effective code review is central to maintaining software quality, yet there is limited research about how the ordering of changed files in Pull Requests (PRs) influences review effectiveness. Most popular code review tools default to alphabetical ordering, favoring predictability over contextual relevance. While prior studies examined how file position shapes reviewer attention, it remains unclear how such ordering influences cognitive load and perceived review thoroughness. This study presents the first large-scale survey of 1,355 professional developers across 182 widely used open-source projects to investigate how file ordering impacts review behavior, comprehension, and perceived effectiveness. Our mixed-methods analysis reveals that only 10.2% of reviewers consider alphabetical ordering optimal, underscoring a cognitive misalignment in their interpretation of code changes. Although some developers appreciate its predictability, more than half (57.6%) report that it increases context switching, disrupts logical reasoning, and contributes to review fatigue, and 63.9% expressed concern that the default ordering may cause them to miss bugs. We further identify key challenges in multi-file reviews and elicit developers’ expectations for improved tooling, including dependency-aware grouping and customizable file ordering (requested by 66% of reviewers). These findings highlight the need for reviewer-centric interface designs that better align tool behavior with human cognition.

title: "Making Our Life Less Monotonous" or "Just Tick Things Off": An Exploratory Multi-Method Study of Toil
abstract: Google introduced Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) as a DevOps approach focused on service reliability. A key concept in SRE is toil defined as manual, repetitive, automatable, and reactive tasks that arise in production service management, scale with service growth, and provide no lasting value. As SRE adoption expands beyond Google, organisations adapt SRE practices and terminology, leading to inconsistencies in how toil is defined and perceived.

title: A Strategy-based Framework for Exploratory Playtesting in Open-World Games
abstract: Bugs in video games can frustrate players and compromise product success. Ensuring quality in these complex, dynamic systems requires systematic testing practices grounded in software engineering. While automated testing has advanced in other domains, games still depend on manual playtesting to capture the player’s experience and detect emergent behaviors that automation cannot easily replicate. This research proposes xPloiT, a strategy-based framework for exploratory playtesting. The framework organizes testing through domain-specific strategies that guide playtesters in planning, executing and documenting test sessions. The resulting structured playtraces will serve as data for modeling agentic playtesting systems that emulate exploratory behaviors. xPloiT aims to create human-like agents capable of reproducing real testing behaviors, contributing to both human-informed and semi-automated testing in complex game environments.

title: Architecture Conformance Checking for Microservice-based Systems
abstract: Microservice-based architectures (MSA) offer scalability, flexibility, and modularity, but their distributed and heterogeneous nature increases the risk of architectural deviation and erosion. Ensuring consistency between the planned and implemented architecture, known as Architectural Conformance Checking (ACC), is particularly challenging in MSA due to their distributed nature, heterogeneous technologies, and dynamic communication mechanisms. This research proposes an AI-assisted approach for ACC in MSA, addressing both structural and behavioral dimensions. This work aims to advance the state of the art by integrating AI into the ACC process, improving automation, accuracy, and scalability in architectural conformance verification.

title: Tailoring Software Engineering Generative AI Agents to Company Standards and Developers’ Preferences
abstract: One of the hurdles of integrating generative AI (GenAI) tools into existing software engineering workflows is that the outputs generated by the foundational models are not tailored to specific company standards and developers’ individual preferences. This challenge has prevented many companies from adopting AI-assisted software engineering across their workflows. This PhD project aims therefore at investigating in the next three years different methods and tools for providing tailored and personalized GenAI outputs taking both company standards and developers’ preferences into account. The objective is to facilitate GenAI integration into existing software engineering workflows and boost adoption across different software engineering activities.

title: Towards Automatic Software Faults Analysis
How do Compiler Bugs Affect OS Kernels
abstract: Compiler bugs can silently introduce bugs into their compiled code. Although compiler bugs are critical in the development of OS kernels, most studies on compiler bugs analyze the characteristics of only compiler bugs themselves. Their findings are less interesting to outsiders, e.g., the OS community. Although two recent papers have started to analyze how compiler bugs affect the development of other projects, no study has been conducted to explore how such bugs affect OS kernels. As a result, many questions are still open. For instance, in the development of OS kernels, are most compiler bugs identified by OS programmers themselves? When bypassing compiler bugs, what is the relationship between compiler-bug symptoms and modified OS components? The answers to the above questions are useful for both compiler and OS programmers. To answer the above questions, we conducted the first empirical study on how compiler bugs affect OS kernels. We collected 494 workarounds of compiler bugs from the revision histories of 7 popular OS kernels. We analyzed these workarounds and explored the answers to these research questions. We have summarized some findings according to our early results. For instance, we found that in most workarounds, compiler bugs are not reported by OS programmers.

title: Understanding the Executability of Example Code in Hugging Face Model Cards: An Empirical Study
Hierarchical Metamorphic Test Oracles for Agent Evaluation
abstract: As autonomous systems transition from data-driven components to intent-driven agents that reason, plan, and act, traditional testing approaches become inadequate. Agents produce execution traces, and correctness depends on hierarchical intent spanning goals, strategies, and actions. We present MESA (Metamorphic Evaluation of Systems and Agents), a modular framework that adapts metamorphic testing principles to agent evaluation through three oracle layers (Goal, Strategy, and Action) that verify consistency relations across abstraction levels. Unlike binary success metrics, MESA decomposes failures by level, enabling targeted debugging. Our framework establishes metamorphic relations as a principled approach to agent testing, providing theoretical foundations and practical tooling for testing modern agentic systems.

title: Applying Neuroinclusive Agile Practices in Software Engineering Team-Based Learning
abstract: Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion have become increasingly relevant in Software Engineering, yet neurodiversity remains underexplored, particularly in educational contexts. This study presents the pilot application of a Catalog of Neuroinclusive Recommendations for Agile Software Engineering Teams, comprising 34 practices applied in undergraduate IT courses. The catalog was derived from prior literature and studies on challenges faced by developers with Autism Spectrum Disorder and Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder. Using an action research approach, we examined the feasibility, benefits, and challenges of applying these recommendations in student teams. The results indicate potential for improving productivity, communication, and inclusion in software engineering education.

title: Exploring the Information Disorientation Problem in Automated Program Repair under Relaxed Localization
abstract: Automated Program Repair (APR) is essential for reducing manual debugging effort and enhancing software reliability. However, traditional approaches rely on precise fault localization, which is costly and often unavailable. Given that many bugs exhibit fuzzy boundaries and wide fix spans, we conduct a preliminary study on APR under relaxed localization constraints. Our findings reveal that Large Language Models (LLMs) struggle in these settings due to chaotic or insufficient context—a challenge we define as Information Disorientation. To address this, we propose a novel APR approach that integrates logical decomposition, fine-grained context retrieval, and block-to-whole reasoning. Preliminary experiments demonstrate that our method effectively mitigates information disorientation.

title: Bridging the Final Gap: Fuzzing Template Generation from Protocol Reverse Engineering
abstract: Security testing for proprietary or undocumented protocols is particularly challenging, as it depends on reverse-engineering techniques to infer protocol formats. This process involves analyzing network traffic or program binaries to deduce message structures and semantics. However, the resulting specifications cannot be directly used as input for fuzzing. To enable efficient automated security testing, a crucial conversion step is required: systematically transforming the reverse-engineered format specifications into PEACH-compatible Pit file. To address this need, this paper presents PRE2Fuzz, an extensible and integrated protocol analysis and conversion system. PRE2Fuzz integrates multiple reverse-engineering tools, supports parallel analysis, and automatically converts the inferred results into executable Pit file, thereby bridging the gap between protocol reverse engineering and automated fuzzing. Evaluations demonstrate the system’s practicality and generality: tests using PRE2Fuzz-generated Pit templates on eight widely used protocols achieved branch coverage.

title: Unsupervised Approaches to Futile Cycle Detection in AI Agents
abstract: Like traditional software, AI agents are prone to failure; specifically, they can enter ‘repetitive futile cycles’—loops of unproductive behavior that are particularly difficult to detect. This paper introduces the concept of futile cycles and distinguishes them from productive cycles in agent execution trajectories. We propose unsupervised approaches for detecting futile cycles that leverage both structural and semantic representations of agent trajectories evaluated on a large dataset of 1575 trajectories for a LangGraph-based stock market multi-Agent application. Our hybrid approach achieves an F1 score of 0.72 (precision: 0.62, recall: 0.86), significantly outperforming individual structural (F1: 0.08) and semantic (F1: 0.28) methods.

title: Y-Map: A Multi-Encoder Y-Architecture for Predicting Performance-Aware Object-Relational Mappings
Technical Briefing on Qualitative Data Analysis and Theory Development
abstract: This technical briefing will enable ICSE attendees to gain hands-on experience with conducting systematic and rigorous qualitative data analysis using socio-technical grounded theory (STGT), and learn the basics of theory development as an advanced practice in qualitative SE research. Aimed at students and professional researchers with all levels of experience, it will equip attendees with the knowledge, skills, and resources required to handle qualitative data from human and LLM sources, and to derive rich descriptive findings, taxonomies, theoretical frameworks, models, and theories.

title: Textbook-Embedded Virtual Teaching Assistant That Answers CS1 Questions With Verifiable Citations
abstract: Students in CS1 often struggle to find course-appropriate answers across scattered resources and may not know how to ask questions due to hidden knowledge gaps. We present a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) Virtual Teaching Assistant(VTA) that extracts knowledge from course materials to answer exam and conceptual questions with CS1-aligned explanations and verifiable textbook citations. Experiments show reliable, complete responses with correct links to relevant textbook sections. Usage logs and surveys indicate that students ask more conceptual than problem-solving questions, and 89% report that the assistant is helpful—suggesting that grounded LLM support can encourage deeper engagement with core concepts.

title: Toward Intelligent, Reliable, and Secure Automation of CI/CD Workflows
abstract: CI/CD pipelines form a core component of contemporary software engineering, automating key stages of the development lifecycle. Since its release in 2019, GitHub Actions (GHA) has rapidly emerged as the dominant CI/CD platform on GitHub, automating millions of workflows daily. However, as the ecosystem grows, developers face persistent challenges in automating GHA workflow creation, mitigating workflow failures, and ensuring security. To address these challenges, my doctoral research systematically examines how developers construct, maintain, and secure GHA workflows in practice, and proposes learning-based approaches to improve their automation quality. The research includes two empirical studies on workflow reliability (reruns and flakiness) and security (evolution of developers’ practices), along with two learning-based frameworks: CIGAR for recommending reusable Actions and FLOWSTEP for generating step-aware workflows. Together, they aim to build an intelligent and secure automation framework for GitHub Actions integrating reliability, security, and semantic understanding.

title: RAGas: Retrieval Augmented Gas Optimization for Smart Contracts with Continuous Knowledge Integration
abstract: Ethereum has gradually become an infrastructure in key areas such as finance, healthcare, and supply chain. When its smart contracts are executed, Gas fees increase with the growth of computational complexity. Therefore, reducing code with high Gas overhead while maintaining functional equivalence is of great significance to deployment costs. Currently available tools rely on fixed rule sets and cannot autonomously adapt to the dynamically evolving patterns of Gas consumption. To this end, we systematically analyzed the grammatical and semantic features that lead to excessive Gas consumption and constructed 12 fine-grained High Gas Consumption (HGC) patterns and knowledge bases covering 6 major categories. Based on this, we propose RAGas, a three-stage retrieval enhancement generation framework that utilizes large language models to locate and automatically fix Gas inefficiency issues. The experimental results show that RAGas can reduce Gas usage by up to 11.2% in real world deployed contracts.

title: Evolving Artificial Ecosystems: Towards the Infusion of Multi-Agent Systems with Inclusive Inheritance
abstract: With recent breakthroughs in the field of large language models, the number of “AI agents” deployed into software systems is growing rapidly. As software systems, they must be continuously modernized to avoid system atrophy. In this paper, we present our early-stage research to infuse multi-agent systems with inclusive inheritance, i.e., with evolutionary principles that rely on both genetic and non-genetic inheritance. As part of this doctoral thesis, we aim to conceptualize and implement inclusive inheritance for software systems and evaluate if this holistic approach leverages the potential of bio-inspired evolution of software systems better than relying only on a selection of evolutionary dimensions.

title: PySTAAR: An End-to-End, Extensible Framework for Automated Python Type Error Repair
abstract: We present PySTAAR, an end-to-end, extensible framework for automatically detecting and repairing type errors in Python programs. PySTAAR integrates test generation, fault localization, patch synthesis, and patch validation into a fully automated pipeline, leveraging large language models and state-of-the-art repair techniques. The framework features a modular, extensible architecture and a user-friendly web interface that visualizes the workflow, making it accessible to developers of all experience levels. We demonstrate that PySTAAR can automatically detect and repair type errors in real-world Python applications, achieving high repair rate without manual intervention. Our tool demonstration is available at https://youtu.be/VizRQsrtsdk.

title: FlakeSync: A Tool for Automatically Repairing Async Flaky Tests
abstract: We present FlakeSync, a tool to automatically repair async flaky tests. Flaky tests can nondeterministically pass or fail when run on the same version of code, misleading developers about the correctness of their code. Async flaky tests are a common type of flaky test in which the test execution asynchronously waits for another parallel computation to complete before proceeding. With an asynchronous wait, the test assumes the other computation will complete within a specific amount of time. However, when the timing is off, the test can fail unexpectedly. FlakeSync repairs async flaky tests by identifying the points during test execution that need to be synchronized to ensure the proper execution. By modifying the code to record when a critical point has been executed and making the test wait until that event occurs, we can ensure proper synchronization. We implement FlakeSync as a Maven plugin, allowing it to be integrable into any Maven project. FlakeSync not only identifies the points that need synchronization during the test execution but also automatically generates a patch implementing the necessary changes for synchronizing the two points. FlakeSync is publicly available on GitHub, and we provide a demo video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gRSFtsO5qm4.

title: The Dynamics of Knowledge Concentration in Long-lived Collaborative Software Codebases
abstract: The organizational factors that govern a development team, such as which parts of the code each developer works on or how code changes are reviewed, are pivotal to the survival of large software codebases. Balancing such organizational factors is an even greater challenge for Free/Libre and Open Source Software (FLOSS) projects, which must sustain hierarchies of maintainers while preventing any of them from becoming overloaded with too much responsibility or concentrating too much knowledge of the codebase. This PhD project aims to identify the effects of different development models on the evolution of knowledge concentration in large, long-lived FLOSS projects. To that end, we envision three phases for the project, each with its expected contribution: (A) A new metric to quantify knowledge concentration considering commit authorship and reviewing duties; (B) A tool to visualize the evolution of knowledge concentration in software codebases; and (C) A taxonomy of patterns of development models for mitigating knowledge-concentration-induced bottlenecks in collaborative codebases.

title: Quantum Software Engineering 101
abstract: Quantum Software Engineering (QSE) focuses on developing cost-effective quantum software for quantum computers. It is a relatively new area of research, with current studies primarily aimed at designing, developing, testing, and maintaining quantum software. Interest in QSE has been steadily increasing; thus, introducing this topic to the ICSE conference audience will further engage young researchers, senior researchers, and practitioners interested in QSE. This technical briefing will introduce quantum computing, followed by the QSE overview. It will then explore QSE in detail from various perspectives, including quantum software requirements engineering, modeling, coding, testing, and debugging. Overall, this technical briefing aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the current state of QSE as well as future research directions.

title: Toward Self-Adaptive and Decentralized Intelligent Software Systems: A Federated Learning Perspective
abstract: Modern software systems are increasingly deployed in large-scale, heterogeneous, and continuously evolving environments. However, traditional software architectures that rely on static configurations and centralized management are insufficient in these settings, as systems must dynamically adapt to runtime changes, diverse data distributions, and varying user contexts. We aim to advance the foundations of self-adaptive and decentralized intelligent software systems capable of rapid deployment, personalized adaptation, and continuous evolution in large-scale heterogeneous environments. In contrast to conventional self-adaptive systems that focus on runtime configuration, our notion of it extends to intelligence-oriented adaptation. Building on this, we explore the architectures and principles that enable these systems to self-organize, adapt, and maintain in dynamic environments. This research envisions a new generation of decentralized intelligent software systems that can autonomously maintain scalability, resilience, and privacy while sustaining long-term adaptability and personalization.

title: Towards a Software Supply Chain Security Barometer: A Model to Assess and Guide Community Efforts
Proofs of Concept as First-Class Architectural Decision Instruments
abstract: Proofs of Concept (PoCs) are used in software-intensive systems to evaluate technologies, reduce uncertainty, and support early decision-making. Despite their role in architectural practice, PoCs remain conceptually underdefined and methodologically ad hoc in both research and practice. In this position paper, we argue that PoCs should be a first-class architectural decision instrument rather than informal experiments or disposable prototypes. We highlight the conceptual ambiguity surrounding PoCs and discuss how this ambiguity undermines architectural decision-making. We then articulate a structured, architecture-centric perspective on PoCs as short-lived, risk-driven experiments explicitly designed to inform architectural choices. Drawing on insights synthesized from academic and grey literature and illustrated through industrial scenarios, we outline a lightweight framework that positions PoCs as repeatable, analyzable, and decision-oriented artifacts. We conclude by surfacing open challenges intended to provoke discussion on how architectural decisions are currently made in practice.

title: LLM-Native Applications: Toward a New Paradigm in Software Engineering
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly embedded into software systems, yet most current solutions are either LLM-based, wrapping an existing system around an LLM, or LLM-augmented, embedding LLMs into existing workflows. These approaches yield quick gains but remain brittle, difficult to reproduce, and poorly governed. We introduce the notion of LLM-native applications: systems conceived from the outset with an LLM as the orchestration core, coordinating tools, memory, knowledge integration, and governance. We present a reference architecture and illustrate feasibility through an LLM-native copilot for literature reviews. We further propose a lifecycle model that highlights how development processes change when LLMs become first-class orchestrators.

title: ARISE: Real-Time Multi-Modal AI for Senior Wellness on Edge Devices
abstract: The global rise in the aging population presents growing challenges for maintaining physical activity, rehabilitation, and independent living. While digital exercise tools have emerged, many fail to balance performance, privacy, and accessibility—particularly for older adults using low-power devices. This paper introduces ARISE, a multi-modal, privacy-preserving AI system that integrates human pose estimation and conversational interaction to create an engaging at-home exercise experience. Implemented entirely on the network edge, ARISE leverages the Raspberry Pi 5 and Hailo-8 Neural Processing Unit (NPU) to achieve real-time, on-device computation without reliance on cloud services. The system combines a YOLOv8m-Pose model for body tracking with a voice-based conversational pipeline using Vosk (speech-to-text), LLaMA (language model), and Kokoro-TTS (speech synthesis) for natural feedback and guidance. Experimental results demonstrate significant reductions in inference latency with NPU acceleration and optimized conversational responsiveness through adaptive chunking and segmentation strategies. The project is open-sourced and available at https://github.com/BlueJayADAL/SCARP25_ARISE.

title: Polaris: MIR-Level Obfuscation in LLVM for Efficient and Robust Decompiler Resistance
abstract: Obfuscation techniques are widely used to hinder program analysis and reverse engineering in order to protect software security and intellectual property. High-level software obfuscation techniques (e.g., source-code- or LLVM IR–based) often leave recognizable artifacts that modern decompilers can effectively exploit, thereby limiting their long-term effectiveness. In contrast, binary-level approaches, although effective, typically incur substantial performance overheads or rely on packing, while still exhibiting structural patterns that remain amenable to automated analysis.

title: SE4AI: Structured AI/ML Enabled Software Development Process
abstract: Most organizations developing software that depends on AI/ML models often rely on ad hoc or unstructured development practices. In many cases, the model and the surrounding software are developed separately, leading to several problems—particularly regarding the quality of the model, the compatibility of the system in which the model is embedded, and the overall suitability of the resulting system to the problem domain. Although prior research has addressed specific aspects of this process and proposed improvements for isolated phases, a comprehensive, quality-oriented development framework is still lacking. This doctoral research aims to propose an enhanced development process that addresses these gaps and opportunities, ensuring both methodological rigor and the delivery of reliable, high-quality AI/ML-enabled systems.

title: From Empathy to Engineering: A Pedagogical Framework and its Authentic mHealth Implementation
abstract: Accessible design is crucial for ensuring equitable access to digital services, yet it remains relegated to elective modules or late-stage compliance in many computing curricula. We propose a human-centered pedagogical framework that embeds inclusive thinking across key phases of the software development process. We introduce two reusable educational tools: a cross-phase persona engine for guiding requirement prioritization and evaluation, and a guideline-reflection instrument that couples accessibility heuristics with structured prompts. The framework is instantiated in an undergraduate course through the redesign of a national mobile health (mHealth) application—a domain where poor accessibility directly exacerbates systemic health inequities. Preliminary pre-course surveys (N = 45) reveal moderate conceptual knowledge of inclusive design but low confidence in its application, underscoring the need for structured longitudinal scaffolding. We discuss the course design, assignments, toolkit and argue that this approach helps students move from abstract empathy to actionable accessibility, offering a framework that can be adapted to other domains.

title: PAGENT: Learning to Patch Software Engineering Issue Fixing Agents
Human-Centered AI for Software Engineering
abstract: The rise of Artificial Intelligence (AI)—especially Generative AI—has transformed software engineering (SE) practices. Yet, SE remains fundamentally human-centered, requiring attention to behavioral, cognitive, and social factors throughout the development life cycle. Despite this, most industrial and academic efforts towards AI integration emphasize technical aspects, hindering practical success. This Ph.D. project aims to develop a scientific understanding of how AI tools, such as Large Language Models, can be integrated into the SE life cycle without compromising software quality or practitioners’ well-being. It investigates the enablers and barriers of AI adoption and their effects on workflow adaptation, particularly within the emerging paradigm of Human-AI teaming. The results will guide practitioners in adopting AI ethically and sustainably, fostering both productivity and well-being.

title: Early Forecasting of Developer Inactivity in Open Source Projects
Reinforcement Learning from Testing Targets for Effective SLM Test Generation
abstract: Unit tests are essential for software reliability, yet their manual construction is time-consuming, motivating automated test generation. To support this task, Small Language Models (SLMs) have been examined as a more efficient and privacy-preserving alternative to larger models, though they often fall short in coverage and fault detection. Recent reinforcement-learning approaches address this limitation, but their effectiveness remains constrained by the use of suite-level reward signals that aggregate the contributions of all generated tests. This coarse feedback limits the model’s ability to learn targeted testing behaviors, such as exercising specific branches or killing individual mutants. To address these issues, we introduce Reinforcement Learning from Testing Targets (RLTT), a target-driven formulation in which SLMs are optimized using reward signals derived from individual testing goals, inspired by search-based software testing. We will study how different target-level reward designs and reinforcement learning algorithms shape the acquisition of goal-directed testing behaviors through an empirical evaluation on real-world applications. The expected contributions include a principled framework for optimizing models for target-driven test generation, guidelines for designing reward signals that capture partial or complete goal achievement, and specialized SLMs capable of generating effective tests for specific targets.

title: System Comprehension and Source Code Manipulation in eXtended Reality
abstract: Comprehending a codebase requires developers to construct mental models spanning multiple levels of abstraction, from architectural overviews to individual components. These components differ across paradigms (e.g., classes in object-oriented systems, functions in functional programming). Software visualization supports this process by translating abstract software structures into perceptually meaningful forms that align with human cognitive processes. When grounded in familiar metaphors, such as cities or landscapes, visualization can further narrow the gap between abstract program constructs and developers’ mental models.

title: Towards Task-Agnostic Evaluation Framework for LLM-Embedded Applications
abstract: Evaluating Large Language Model (LLM) embedded applications presents fundamental challenges distinct from traditional software testing due to non-deterministic behaviour across diverse contexts. Existing benchmarks fail to capture domain-specific requirements, while practitioners resort to ad-hoc strategies that are time-consuming and inconsistent. This research proposes a task-agnostic evaluation framework that automatically synthesises evaluations from reusable principles rather than requiring custom configurations. The framework employs a meta-model capturing essential task properties to enable automated evaluation generation across objective and subjective tasks. Through systematic literature review, grey literature analysis, and practitioner validation, we establish guidelines for evaluation selection across diverse LLM task types. Industry case studies validate the framework’s practical effectiveness, measuring generalizability, performance, time efficiency, and workflow alignment. This research establishes methodological foundations that shift LLM evaluation from task-specific design to systematic synthesis from reusable principles.

title: Trustworthy Resolution of Requirement Conflicts at Runtime
abstract: As software systems become increasingly autonomous, trust has emerged as a critical factor that directly influences users’ acceptance and adoption of these systems. However, trust is challenged by conflicting system requirements, as they can lead to unexpected and potentially unwanted system behaviour. Particularly in autonomous systems that operate in dynamic and uncertain environments, conflicts are likely and need to be managed in a way that preserves and positively impacts the user’s trust. This thesis investigates how conflicting requirements can be managed at runtime in a way that maintains user trust. The resulting contributions aim to establish guidelines for trustworthy conflict management that ensure that conflict resolution is both effective and aligned with user expectations.

title: AgenticTyper: Automated Typing of Legacy Software Projects Using Agentic AI
abstract: Legacy JavaScript systems lack type safety, making maintenance risky. While TypeScript can help, manually adding types is expensive. Previous automated typing research focuses on type inference but rarely addresses type checking setup, definition generation, bug identification, or behavioral correctness at repository scale. We present AgenticTyper, a Large Language Model (LLM)-based agentic system that addresses these gaps through iterative error correction and behavior preservation via transpilation comparison. Evaluation on two proprietary repositories (81K LOC) shows that AgenticTyper resolves all 633 initial type errors in 20 minutes, reducing manual effort from one working day.

title: Architecting Automotive Software for the Emerging Compute-in-the-Network Paradigm
abstract: Emerging compute-capable automotive network switches now allow parts of application functionality to be hosted and executed within the communication fabric, complementing the primary application software execution on electronic control units. This compute-in-the-network paradigm offers opportunities for reducing latency and improving responsiveness in time‑critical automotive systems. However, existing automotive architecture description languages and component models lack abstractions for representing application software residing in network elements, limiting accurate design and analysis. This paper motivates the need to treat the models of onboard network switches as the first-class software architectural entities and outlines research opportunities including unified abstractions, end-to-end timing models extraction, alignment with standards and toolchain interoperability, and addressing new cybersecurity challenges.

title: WiseUT: An Intelligent Framework for Unit Test Generation
abstract: Unit testing is critical but challenging. While LLMs excel at generating readable code, they often struggle with coverage, defect detection, and maintainability. We present WiseUT, an end-to-end framework integrating LLMs with program analysis to address these gaps. WiseUT employs analysis-guided prompting to broaden coverage, type-aware reflective validation to pinpoint genuine defects, and semantic purification for maintainability. Evaluations on open-source and industrial projects demonstrate that WiseUT consistently improves coverage, doubles precision in type error detection, and produces tests preferred by developers. Demo: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DmszXs0eEOE.

title: SoS Governance in Smart Cities: A Tertiary Review Highlighting Research Gaps in the Global South
abstract: Smart cities have evolved into complex systems‑of‑systems (SoS), integrating physical infrastructures, digital platforms, and social processes. Governing such systems poses critical challenges, particularly in the Global South, where socio‑economic conditions, institutional capacity, infrastructural gaps, and inclusion dynamics differ substantially from the Global North. This research conducts a tertiary review to systematically synthesise existing secondary reviews on smart-city governance, with a focus on identifying research gaps specific to the Global South. The study follows the PRISMA methodology to ensure rigor in article selection and employs Design Science Research (DSR) to guide the creation of conceptual and constructive artifacts. Additionally, the Goal-Question-Metric (GQM) model structures data extraction and analysis. Preliminary findings reveal a strong geographic bias toward high-income regions, limited attention to context-sensitive governance frameworks, weak integration of participatory platforms such as digital twins and DAO/Decidim, and a lack of governance mechanisms tailored to the Global South. Expected contributions include a refined research agenda and a structured methodological pathway to support future studies in SoS governance for smart cities in under-represented regions.

title: Anxiety-Aware Requirements Engineering: A Vision Paper
Performance Improvement of Automated Test Input Data Generation by Using Value Concretization
abstract: Automated generation of test input data is a major technical challenge in software engineering research. We are developing a tool for automated test input data generation for COBOL, a language widely used in enterprise applications. As in prior studies, we employ a hybrid approach that combines symbolic execution and constraint solving. In addition, to accommodate the various data representations in COBOL, we introduce a byte-level data representation into the memory model used by our tool. However, this increases constraint complexity and size, leading to degraded solver performance. To address this issue, we propose transforming constraint logic formulae through value concretization. Our evaluation shows that this technique effectively alleviates the performance problem.

title: Software Engineering for Foundation Models (SE4FM)
abstract: Foundation Models (FMs) are among humanity’s most complex software systems. They are currently engineered through tribal knowledge and ad‑hoc processes, despite quarterly release cadences and rapidly expanding model sizes, context lengths, and modalities. This 90‑minute technical briefing presents SE4FM—a disciplined software engineering framing for FMs—organized around four pillars: DataOps (deciding, curating, optimizing, and governing data), ExperimentOps (hypothesis‑driven, scaling‑law‑aware experimentation from small to large; including RLHF/RLAIF/RLVR pipelines), EvalOps (systematic testing, prioritization, and debugging), and FieldOps (releases, monitoring, and compliance). The goal is to give software engineering researchers a unique, insider view of how FMs are really built and run at scale, and to surface concrete SE challenges and opportunities where new SE-centric methods, tools, and theory are urgently needed.

title: What Do We Architect When We Architect LLM Agent Systems?
Agentic Software Engineering: A Roadmap to Software Engineering 3.0
abstract: Software Engineering (SE) is shifting from AI-assisted development (SE 2.0) to Agentic Software Engineering (SE 3.0), where autonomous AI agents act as collaborators. This technical briefing establishes the foundations of a disciplined SE 3.0 practice. We synthesize: (1) a large-scale characterization of agent activity in the wild based on the AIDev dataset, (2) an empirical study of 567 Claude Code pull requests across 157 open-source software projects, and (3) the Structured Agentic Software Engineering (SASE) framework that reframes actors, processes, artifacts, and tools. Attendees will acquire evidence-backed mental models, evaluation patterns for agent-authored PRs, and a practical vocabulary (e.g., agent command environment and agent execution environment) for designing trustworthy human-agent workflows.

title: Power Relationships Effects on Social Sustainability Goals in Software Ecosystems
A Methodological Framework for Intelligent Vulnerability Management in Microservice Architectures
abstract: The widespread adoption of microservices has expanded the attack surface, presenting security challenges that current literature typically addresses through controlled scenarios or synthetic data, thus limiting its applicability in the real world. This research proposes a methodological framework for comprehensive vulnerability management by mining issues in GitHub repositories. Using Natural Language Processing (NLP) techniques, we align real-world vulnerability reports with industry standards such as CVE, CWE, and OWASP, building a hybrid taxonomy that accurately reflects real-world development practices.

title: Comprehensibility-guided Automated Code Refactoring
abstract: Code comprehension is essential for many software engineering tasks, including code refactoring. Although numerous techniques exist for automated refactoring, none explicitly incorporate code comprehensibility as a guiding principle. The goal of this thesis is to enable comprehensibility-guided automated refactoring. To achieve this, we identify three fundamental challenges in current comprehension research: (1) the lack of rigorous, expert-grounded comprehension proxies; (2) the inherent noise in existing proxy measurements; and (3) limitations in current feature sets and models for capturing the cognitive complexity of human code understanding. This thesis addresses these challenges by establishing validated comprehension proxies, developing more robust relative comprehensibility models, and evaluating modern learning methods—including large language models—for predicting code comprehensibility. Ultimately, this work aims to provide a reliable foundation for automated refactoring techniques that explicitly consider the code understandability as a confounding factor for refactoring code.

title: From Metrics to Models: Large Language Models as Human-Aligned Code Readability Evaluators
abstract: Code readability is essential for software maintenance, yet difficult to assess at scale. Traditional metrics fail to capture subjective human judgments, while manual evaluation is expensive and inconsistent. We introduce CoReEval, a benchmark comprising 1.4 million evaluations across 10 LLMs and 656 code snippets (Java, Python, CUDA). We investigate how prompting strategies, decoding parameters, and persona framing influence LLM alignment with human judgments. LLMs exhibit moderate alignment in Java (r=0.25) but near-zero in Python (r=0.02) and CUDA (r=0.00). Developer-guided prompting dramatically improves aspect coverage (Java test Structure: 15% to 94%) but increases score variance. When configured with human-centric criteria, LLMs are promising tools for interpretable code readability assessment in automated code review, developer education, and CI/CD.

title: FastMCC: Multiple-hypotheses Code Completion with Natural Language Phrases as Alternative Suggestions
abstract: LLM-based code completion systems typically offer only one suggestion, often failing to cover developers’ intent, especially with ambiguous context. Current multiple-hypotheses code completion, i.e., generating multiple full-code candidates to increase the possibility to hit the user intent, can mitigate this but with a price of high latency and developers’ cognitive burden. To fill this gap, we propose FastMCC, which presents multiple hypotheses as concise natural language phrases instead of full code. It uses a two-stage inference: first generating an initial code suggestion followed by alternative intent phrases; then generating intent-aligned code if a phrase is selected. We design a lightweight fine-tuning framework to equip base code LLMs with this capability without compromising their original code completion performance. Experiments on three code LLMs show FastMCC maintains the pass rate of initial suggestions, while saving 76.6% generated tokens for multiple-hypotheses options.

title: An Empirical Study on Maintenance and Evolution Processes of Embedded Software
abstract: Embedded software is pervasive in safety-critical domains, including healthcare, automotive, aerospace, and the Internet of Things (IoT). Its maintenance and evolution are challenging due to hardware constraints, real-time requirements, and long life cycles, often exceeding 10–20 years. Studies indicate that 60–90% of software costs are related to evolution and maintenance. However, empirical evidence shows that current industrial practices remain fragmented, lacking integrative processes and specialized tools. This doctoral research addresses this gap by combining a systematic literature review (SLR), an industry survey, and the design of an integrative process supported by a software tool. The work will be validated in a real-world medical scenario: a low-cost insulin infusion pump. Preliminary results highlight heterogeneity in industrial practices, lack of standardized metrics, and difficulties in handling technical debt and obsolescence. The expected contributions include a unified process, an operational tool, and empirical evidence from both industry and academia.

title: Interpretable AI with MLIR (IAM):A Unified Framework for Neural Network Transparency
abstract: Modern AI interpretability tools operate in isolation, each requiring separate forward passes and adding significant latency, making real-time AI safety auditing impractical. This research addresses fragmentation by treating interpretability as a first-class compilation primitive. IAM (Interpretable AI with MLIR) unifies fragmented tools into a single compiler-integrated framework built on JAX’s vertically integrated architecture. By defining custom MLIR dialects for sparse autoencoders, attribution, and policy steering, and leveraging compiler optimization through XLA’s fusion and memory planning, IAM eliminates redundant computation. The framework introduces skip-transcoder architectures for real-time steering while maintaining model accuracy. This work establishes the foundation for trustworthy AI systems where interpretability is engineered through rigorous compiler abstractions.

title: Toward an ISO-Based Epistemic Capability Framework for Specializing LLMs Through Knowledge and Reasoning Integration for Software Artifact Generation
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are capable to assist software artifact construction, but current limitations are attributed to the lack of specialized domain knowledge and the inability to modulate reasoning, which is mostly supplied through user prompt interactions.

title: Automated Testing of Conversational Agents with Chatbot Dōjō
abstract: Conversational agents (or chatbots) interact in natural language, and may provide access to software services for specific tasks, like ordering food or obtaining customer support. Given their prominence and ubiquity, they need to be reliable. However, automated chatbot testing techniques, able to cope with the large variety of existing chatbot technologies, are missing.

title: Vibe Engineering
abstract: “Vibe coding” represents a paradigm shift where non-technical users, or “software makers”, create applications by describing the desired outcome, focusing entirely on the final output rather than the underlying code. This movement, propelled by hyper-growth platforms like Lovable, Bubble, and Glide, actualizes the vision of “AIware”: software for all, by all. However, this remarkable progress is currently confined to applications of limited complexity and introduces significant risks of unreliability and failure. This 90-minute technical briefing introduces Vibe Engineering, a structured framework for AI-assisted software creation that goes beyond one-shot prompts. The framework operates by defining roles, specifying artifacts, and orchestrating a repeatable process. It is built on two foundational pillars: (1) Intent Engineering, which focuses on deeply understanding user needs through multi-agent dialogues, Theory of Mind (ToM) principles, and test-driven requirement refinement; and (2) Realization Engineering, a specialized Agent Execution Environment (AEE) where multi-agent teams autonomously build, test, and verify the software based on the user’s validated intent. This briefing provides an insider’s view of the technical challenges in this domain and surfaces concrete software engineering research opportunities.

title: The Energy Consumption of Legacy COBOL Systems: A Forgotten Direction and COBJoules Tool
abstract: The increasing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into everyday tasks has driven demand for high-performance software to an unprecedented level. This has resulted in an exponential growth in energy consumption by software systems. While extensive research has been done focusing on measuring and evaluating the energy consumption of machine learning and AI systems, particularly in Python, a significant gap remains in tools and methodologies for assessing energy usage in legacy systems. Legacy software systems continue to underpin critical operations across industries such as finance, government, and healthcare, yet their energy consumption remains largely unmeasured and unoptimized. As organizations face mounting pressure to improve sustainability and reduce operational costs, the lack of dedicated tools for quantifying the energy usage of legacy codebases, particularly those written in languages such as COBOL, has become a significant barrier. In this paper, we discuss this critical challenge and specifically focus on the legacy language of COBOL. In particular, we present COBJoules as one of the first tools designed to measure and analyze energy consumption in COBOL environments. The tool was evaluated using benchmark tasks from Rosetta Code, demonstrating its effectiveness in quantifying energy consumption patterns for COBOL. The tool and all related artifacts can be found at https://github.com/rishalab/COBJoules.

title: Intelligent Approach for Fostering Research Collaborations between Academia and Industry
Exploring Prompts as Mixed Requirements and Solutions Artifacts
abstract: AI coding assistants shift software practice from writing code to crafting prompts. We argue that prompts should be treated as lightweight, evolving requirement artifacts that intentionally mix in information from the solution space. We propose a simple conceptual model – the Prompt Triangle – with three components: Functionality and Quality (the requirement), General Solutions (solution strategy and technology choices) and Specific Solutions (implementation-level constraints). We hypothesize that prompts evolve across these components, are shaped by user factors, stabilize on functionality over time, and that completeness across all three components correlates with code quality. We outline an empirical agenda to test these hypotheses through corpus creation, longitudinal studies, controlled experiments and the development of requirements-aware prompting guidelines.

title: Games Designed to Teach or Practice Technical Debt Management: A Systematic Mapping Study
abstract: Technical Debt (TD) refers to accumulated software issues that result from shortcuts and other suboptimal decisions during software development and maintenance. Companies and educators increasingly seek effective ways to train current and future employees in managing TD. Games have emerged as an innovative approach to teaching and practicing Technical Debt Management (TDM) activities both in industry and education. Games have the power to impact practitioners’ ability to understand TD in Software Engineering. This systematic mapping study examines such games. The primary goal is to identify all relevant games that support TDM learning and practice, regardless of the target audience.

title: Engineering MLOps for Adversarial Edge Networks in Agricultural Deployments
abstract: Deploying machine learning in distributed edge environments where participants are economic competitors presents fundamental challenges unaddressed by traditional MLOps frameworks. Existing federated learning assumes collaborative participants with reliable connectivity, while differential privacy applies uniform protection regardless of competitive relationships. In agricultural deployments, farms growing identical crops compete in commodity markets yet benefit from shared model training—requiring privacy guarantees that prevent competitive intelligence leakage without destroying model utility. We present an MLOps architecture for adversarial edge networks, contributing: (1) adaptive privacy budgets that allocate differential privacy protection based on competitive overlap between participants, (2) time-window aggregation with convergence under multi-day network partitions, and (3) edge-based data quality validation that identifies corrupted sensor readings before distributed training. Production deployment across agricultural edge networks demonstrates that adaptive privacy demonstrates a tunable trade-off, achieving 84.2% accuracy in high-competition scenarios (preventing 77% of attacks) compared to 97.8% in low-competition settings. Time-window aggregation enables graceful degradation of model utility during multi-day partitions, maintaining a stable but reduced performance profile.

title: A Multi-Modal Robotic Framework for Physical GUI Interaction Testing
abstract: Automated testing of mobile applications remains challenging when realistic user interactions must be reproduced and GUI behavior verified without relying on invasive mechanisms such as instrumentation or ADB-level control. Existing approaches, including DLD and R-DLD, detect data loss triggered by activity restarts but still depend on system-level access, which limits their applicability on real devices.

title: Trustworthiness of Continuous Integration Practices
Automating Code-Change Rationale Generation to Support Software Maintenance Tasks
abstract: Understanding the reasons(rationale) behind code changes is essential for effective software maintenance, yet developers often struggle with fragmented documentation and the absence of clear, actionable rationale explanations. This research aims to bridge that gap by enabling fine-grained, personalized, and task-specific explanations of why code changes occur. We (1) develop techniques to extract and generate multi-document, fine-grained rationale summaries, (2) model developer profiles to tailor explanations to their expertise and familiarity, and (3) generate task-specific rationales for activities such as code review, debugging, and onboarding. Together, this work contributes new empirical insights, a cross-artifact and fine-grained rationale benchmark, and an automated tool for personalized, task-aware rationale generation to advance developer understanding and support software maintenance.

title: Technical Optimizations on Textbook-Efficient Code with LLMs
abstract: Runtime efficiency is an important attribute of source code, typically improved through high-level algorithm selections or low-level implementation optimizations. While algorithmic efficiency is well studied and formally taught, technical optimization on implementation details relies heavily on tacit, experience-driven knowledge that is often inaccessible to novices. To examine this assumption, we prompted six LLMs to optimize 649 student programs that were already efficient by textbook standards. Among the LLM-generated outputs that preserved the original functionality, \(34\%\) achieved non-trivial runtime improvements, with an average execution time reduction of \(18.9\%\) and a corresponding speedup of 1.3 ×. This finding indicates a potential gap between being textbook-efficient and being practically efficient.

title: LLM-Assisted Uncertainty Identification in Self-Adaptive Robotics
abstract: Understanding uncertainties present in complex systems, such as self-adaptive robotics, their potential impacts, and mitigation strategies has always been a major challenge for researchers and industry professionals. This hands-on technical briefing will present novel approaches, a tool, and a taxonomy to systematically and automatically identify uncertainty in self-adaptive robotics using large language models (LLMs). The content of this briefing is being developed as part of an EU project named RoboSAPIENS, which aims at ensuring the trustworthiness of self-adaptive robots. To assist industry professionals in the uncertainty identification process, we developed an LLM-based uncertainty identification approach and implemented it in a tool. This briefing will cover LLM-based uncertainty identification, prompting techniques, uncertainty taxonomy, hands-on tool sessions, and experiences from our interactions with industry professionals.

title: Reframing Software Architecture and Design Skills in the Era of Generative Artificial Intelligence
abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is part of mainstream software development, including software architecture (e.g., for generating architecture documentation or exploring architectural decisions). We argue that GenAI not only impacts how architects work and the artifacts they produce, but GenAI also affects (i) skills required of software architects to properly use GenAI for software architecture activities, and (ii) skill development (e.g., how to move from junior to senior engineer without sufficient hands-on experience due to “delegating” work to GenAI or the risk of “de-skilling” of senior architects by relying on too much on GenAI without critical reflection). We therefore propose a new research direction to understand and support software architecture and design skills in the era of GenAI.

title: Catching License Changes Before They Cost: Leveraging LLMs to Analyze License Evolution in Open Source Software
Preventing Failures of Smart Human-Centric Ecosystems
abstract: Smart Human-centric Ecosystems (SHEs), like smart cities, emerge from the co-existence of heterogeneous systems with independently defined specifications. SHEs may fail despite the correct behavior of the systems that comprise the SHE, yet current approaches overlook the critical need of ensuring the reliability of SHEs.

title: T-Wise Sample Comparison with Binary Decision Diagrams
abstract: Testing configurable systems is challenging, as faults often result from interactions between multiple features. Therefore, quality assurance also requires to test configurations including such interactions. T-wise sampling techniques generate sets of configurations to cover each valid interaction among t features. However, state-of-the-art techniques fail to scale to large systems, such as automotive02_v4 with ≈ 18, 000 features. Moreover, the diversity of sampling techniques results in a variety of different samples, raising the question of which sample to use for testing. We aim to tackle this question by introducing a Binary Decision Diagram (BDD)-based metric for assessing sample quality. The characteristics of the metric can further be used as a guide for ideas to enhance a sample’s quality. As a cornerstone of our BDD-based work, we introduce a counting free algorithm for computing the atomic sets—features that are constrained to always be (de)selected together—serving as a preprocessing step for efficient and deterministic BDD compilation.

title: TenderChat with Dynamic RAG: A Prompt-Adaptive RAG Framework for Australian Government Tender Analysis
abstract: The Australian tendering process demands searching through many individual documents to understand the requirements. Currently deployed methods of keyword and ID searching are limited in their ability to discover new tender opportunities. While large language models (LLMs) are powerful, they lack access to real-time, structured tender information. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) offers a solution by combining LLMs with a knowledge base, enabling semantic search and factual responses with reduced hallucinations. In this study, we present TenderChat: a novel conversational chatbot framework that utilises query enhancement and dynamic prompting to retrieve relevant information and generate accurate responses efficiently. TenderChat’s framework utilises multiple prompt-engineered LLMs to understand queries contextually and categorise them for the deployment of lightweight, specialised prompts in response generation. This system is benchmarked using RAGAs, BERT Score, and four specialised LLM-Judges to evaluate domain-specific metrics. Our proposed framework is also adapted for the MultiDoc2Dial dataset, enabling the evaluation of multi-turn conversations with reference answers. TenderChat offers a practical and scalable RAG framework for conversational retrieval and explanation of government tenders, deploying a novel Dynamic RAG approach. Demo: https://youtu.be/EYDL74MYmhY

title: Green AI by Default: Energy Reduction Techniques for LLMs in SE
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly being applied to Software Engineering (SE) tasks, showing high accuracy in various problems. However, their high computational demands and energy consumption raise sustainability concerns and hinder their use on consumer hardware and resource-constrained platforms. Multiple optimization techniques exist, but they are often neglected due to the technical difficulty of applying them during model development. This research aims to improve the accessibility of optimization techniques by (1) making energy reporting of LLM more accessible, (2) streamlining and automating optimization techniques, (3) providing guidelines to select appropriate techniques for different use cases, and (4) exploiting these techniques to design efficient SLM ensemble architectures for LLM-enabled applications. Expected contributions include methods for measuring and reporting energy usage, tools to automate compression of models, guidelines to guide developers through the optimization process, and using these results to explore alternative deployment setups for compressed LLMs.

title: Exploring Large Language Models for Compliance Violation Detection in Android Apps
abstract: Privacy regulations (GDPR, LGPD, PDPA, PIPEDA) impose compliance requirements on mobile applications; verifying code-level adherence remains labor-intensive. We present the first evaluation of Language Models (LLMs) for detecting privacy compliance violations in Android applications. We construct annotated datasets spanning four regulations with 57 to 146 instances each, and evaluate four LLMs on violation localization (file, module, and line levels) and snippet-level classification. Experiments reveal granularity-dependent model specialization: Claude variants excel at coarse-grained analysis (MAP up to 0.66) while GPT-4o demonstrates superior fine-grained detection (Acc@1 0.48), alongside performance disparities—GDPR and PIPEDA yield twice the scores of LGPD and PDPA. These findings provide grounding for designing hybrid compliance verification systems.

title: Rate My Web Design? Using LLMs to Predict Human Subjective Ratings of Generated Web UI Prototypes
abstract: GenAI services are being increasingly employed in UI/UX engineering, whose automation remains insufficiently advanced compared to other Software Engineering activities. The iterative process involves creating and assessing UI prototypes, but up-to-date GUI Agents lack in evaluating subjective quality dimensions like aesthetics. We had ChatGPT and RateMyImage (RMI) rate 84 web AI-generated UI prototypes, and then benchmarked their ratings with human ones, provided by 39 HCI experts. RMI rated the most similarly to humans (r = 0.546), while GPT-4o showed poor agreement with human participants and poor internal consistency. The best (AIC-optimal) regression model for humans’ subjective ratings that incorporated both pre-LLM UI features and models’ ratings had R2=0.423. We also provide some preliminary guidelines for UI/UX engineers seeking to involve AI in assessing design prototypes.

title: Teaching Emotional Awareness in Software Engineering: Evidence from a Professional Training Program
abstract: Emotional awareness—recognizing one’s own and others’ emotions—is critical for software engineering teamwork, yet teaching it remains unexplored. We investigate how an emotional awareness tool, combining biometric and self-reported data, can support team reflection during agile retrospectives in a professional training program. Through an empirical study, we find that participants valued the tool for individual self-reflection but not for team collaboration, due to reluctance to share emotions in newly formed teams. Our results suggest that educational programs should focus on building individual emotional self-awareness first, which may later enhance professional teamwork once students are comfortable with recognizing and reflecting on their emotions in the team setting.

title: From Collaboration to Team Effectiveness: The Role of Emergent States in Distributed and Dynamic Software Teams
abstract: Collaboration in software engineering (SE) is increasingly challenged by interdisciplinary, distributed and dynamic team structures, yet most SE research and tooling continue to overlook the emergent dynamics of team effectiveness and their relational foundation. This study aims to develop a socio-technical construct model of collaboration, based on qualitative analysis of SE professionals’ experiences and rooted in organizational psychology theory and software engineering research. By examining how emergent team properties like psychological safety, trust, and shared understanding relate to collaboration processes and outcomes, the research aims to produce a refined conceptual framework, as well as actionable guidance for supporting team effectiveness in complex SE settings. Preliminary results reveal that affective mediators are central to effective collaboration, but are rarely systematically operationalized in practice. The work seeks feedback from the SE community on refining construct definitions, designing rigorous qualitative studies, and translating these insights into comprehensive, yet accessible support for collaborative work in software projects.

title: An Incident Management Approach Based on Site Reliability Engineering Practices to Support Governance in Proprietary Software Ecosystems
abstract: This study investigates how Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) practices can enhance incident management as a governance mechanism within Proprietary Software Ecosystems (PSECO). These ecosystems operate under contractual, regulatory, and intellectual property constraints that complicate collaboration and reliability assurance. To address this challenge, we adopted a structured empirical design grounded in Empirical Software Engineering principles, combining a systematic mapping study, a multivocal literature review, and a participative case study with a global organization. The results led to the design the Supported Integration Approach (SIA) aimed at integrating human expertise, process, and technological enablers. Early findings indicate that the approach improves incident traceability and knowledge transfer among teams while aligning reliability practices with governance objectives. This research contributes theoretical, methodological, and practical insights for embedding SRE practices into PSECO governance, promoting a sustainable environment.

title: Modular Workshop Architecture for Teaching Machine Learning in Autonomous Driving by Non-Experts
abstract: Machine learning (ML) literacy is increasingly seen as a core educational goal, yet hands-on ML teaching remains difficult in K-12 and introductory settings. Challenges include making ML pipeline stages and their interdependencies understandable, enabling rapid experimentation and iteration, and keeping workshops feasible for teachers without deep ML or robotics expertise. Many existing platforms either require substantial technical skills or hide the pipeline, limiting both conceptual understanding and experimental learning.

title: Bridging Theory and Practice: Ethical AI User Story Generator - Translating Ethical AI Requirements into Ethical User Stories
abstract: While the subject of ethical guidelines for AI is widely discussed, there is often a lack of practical application in the context of software development. In order to address this issue, we present EAI-USG, a tool that automatically translates high-level ethical requirements into Ethical User Stories, transforming ethical principles into concrete tasks within agile workflows. Powered by large language models with retrieval-augmented generation, the tool produces structured stories that practitioners perceive as clear and useful. A preliminary evaluation involving 30 software professionals suggests that this approach facilitates the operationalization of ethics during requirements engineering with only a minor additional effort.

title: SIKG: A Semantic Impact Knowledge Graph Approach for Adaptive Test Selection and Prioritization
LLM-Augmented Program Analysis: Towards Practical and Scalable Bug Detection
abstract: Static program analysis plays a fundamental role in software engineering and security, yet practical tools continue to struggle with the long-standing trade-off between precision and scalability. Recent progress in large language models (LLMs) offers new opportunities to enhance program reasoning, but their integration with formal analysis remains largely unexplored. This proposal investigates how LLMs can augment static analysis to improve the practicality and precision of bug and vulnerability detection. Two completed studies, LLift (OOPSLA’24) and BugLens (ASE’25), demonstrate that structured LLM reasoning can significantly reduce false positives and uncover real bugs in the Linux kernel. Building on these results, the ongoing research seeks to design hybrid frameworks that enable principled collaboration between LLMs and static analyzers, and to characterize the theoretical limits of LLM-based reasoning. Ultimately, this work aims to advance neuro-symbolic program analysis toward practical and trustworthy software reasoning.

title: Towards Cognitive-Agent-Driven Prompt Optimization for Automated Program Repair
abstract: Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have significantly reshaped software engineering workflows, particularly in Automated Program Repair (APR). Despite their potential, LLM-based repair techniques often exhibit unstable behavior, limited generalization and strong prompt sensitivity. This proposal investigates a research direction that unifies Reinforcement Learning (RL), cognitive agents and self-adaptive architectures to autonomously optimize prompts for LLM-based patch generation. We hypothesize that treating prompt design as an adaptive optimization problem can significantly improve stability and correctness. By embedding prompt refinement in a continuous feedback loop, and enabling agents to maintain persistent beliefs extracted from repositories and execution traces, the repair process becomes more stable, explainable and effective.

title: Execution-Aware Code Documentation through Semantic Data Differences
abstract: Automated code documentation has gained increasing importance as AI-assisted software engineering tools become integrated into the software lifecycle. However, most approaches rely solely on static features of code, overlooking its dynamic behavior—particularly in data-centric programming environments where code meaning is deeply tied to its effect on data. This research explores how execution-aware code documentation can be achieved by introducing semantic data differences, a structured symbolic representation of how code execution transforms data. By capturing these runtime semantics, this work aims to extend code understanding beyond syntax and lexical features. I propose a multimodal modeling framework that combines static code analysis with post-execution semantics. In support of this framework, I design a data collection pipeline that executes real-world data-centric notebooks, logs variable-level changes, and abstracts them into a grammar of semantic data differences for training and evaluation. This ongoing doctoral research aims to enable documentation systems that describe not only how code is written, but also what code does to data—a step toward more transparent, reproducible, and intelligent data-centric software.

title: JUnitGenie: A Framework for Path-Sensitive Unit Test Generation with Large Language Models
Technical Briefing on Beyond A/B Testing - Orthogonal and Experimental Designs
